headline: KSE-100 sheds 1,138 points on profit-taking as Hormuz tanker attacks spike oil and rattle Wall Street, even as Pakistan locks in a $1.2bn IMF staff-level deal
mood: Risk-off tape · Hormuz oil spike and a hawkish Fed collide with local profit-taking

five_things.chip: KSE-100 Retreats From Record Highs on Profit-Taking
five_things.html: The KSE-100 shed 1,138.50 points (−0.68%) to close at 167,441.90 on Thursday, reversing from an intraday high of 169,486.60 as banking and fertiliser heavyweights led late selling. Traded volume fell to roughly 152.07 million shares worth Rs17.72 billion (from 244.16 million shares/Rs22.37 billion on Wednesday), with decliners thumping advancers 81 to 18 (1 unchanged) among index constituents. United Bank (−152.76 index points), Fauji Fertilizer (−85.51), Systems Limited (−54.28), Engro Fertilizers (−54.06) and Pakistan Oilfields (−47.84) capped the index, while Pakistan State Oil (+32.84), Lotte Chemical (+13.54) and Abbott Laboratories (+7.18) were the lone bright spots as refiners rode the crude spike. Business Recorder and Pakera confirm the levels.
five_things.sentiment: sharp pullback despite an IMF relief headline

five_things.chip: Pakistan, IMF Reach Staff-Level Deal, Unlocking $1.2bn
five_things.html: The IMF and Islamabad reached a staff-level agreement on 7 October completing the 2026 Article IV consultation alongside the fourth EFF review and third RSF review, clearing the way for roughly $1.2 billion (about $1.0bn/SDR 760mn under the EFF and $210mn/SDR 154mn under the RSF) once the Executive Board signs off. The Fund's mission, led by Iva Petrova, held talks in Karachi and Islamabad from 23 September to 7 October, and continues to press for exchange-rate flexibility as a shock absorber even as the rupee held broadly steady at 277.01 interbank. ProPakistani and the IMF confirm the terms.
five_things.sentiment: policy win, tranche release still pending board approval

five_things.chip: Crude Spikes on Hormuz Tanker Attacks, Hits US Tech
five_things.html: Brent rose 4.0% to settle at $104.28 and WTI gained 3.6% to $91.49 on Thursday after Iran escalated attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with a Gulf of Mexico storm threat adding a secondary squeeze; prices eased off session highs after President Trump said Washington would not strike Iran before the November midterms. The inflation scare helped drag the Nasdaq down 1.25% to 27,193.34 and the S&P 500 down 0.47% to 7,765.36, while the Dow eked out a 0.10% gain to 51,231.64 as energy names offset tech weakness; a Financial Times report trimming OpenAI's revenue estimate added separate pressure on semiconductors. CNBC and Yahoo Finance confirm the levels.
five_things.sentiment: geopolitical supply risk revives inflation jitters

five_things.chip: Fed Keeps Hike Door Open as Waller Flags More Tightening
five_things.html: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, though the timing remains flexible, keeping alive the hawkish path set by September's first hike since 2023 to 3.75–4.00%. Futures markets price roughly 81–83% odds of a hold at the 28 October FOMC meeting but still assign better-than-75% odds of a hike at the 9 December meeting, consistent with 16 of 18 FOMC members' dot-plot projections for at least one more 2026 move; the 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5.23% and the 2-year near 4.77%. CNBC and Schwab confirm the stance.
five_things.sentiment: higher-for-longer narrative intact, oil the new catalyst

five_things.chip: Gulf Non-Oil Engines Accelerate as PIF Unveils 2026–30 Plan
five_things.html: Gulf diversification kept outrunning the headlines: the S&P Global UAE PMI held at 55.3 in September on the fastest output growth since February, while Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI jumped to 55.3 from 53.8 in August, a seven-month high, even as business expectations softened on regional-tension risk. Separately, Saudi Arabia's PIF approved its 2026–2030 strategy, directing roughly 80% of capital into domestic investments (scaled back from a 30% foreign-allocation peak to 20%) across three portfolios anchored by tourism, NEOM and advanced manufacturing. AGBI and PIF confirm the details.

matrix.local_html: Pakistan's tape gave back Wednesday's gains: the KSE-100 fell 1,138.50 points (−0.68%) Thursday to close at 167,441.90, reversing from an intraday high of 169,486.60 as profit-taking hit banks and fertilisers — United Bank, Fauji Fertilizer, Systems Limited and Engro Fertilizers were the heaviest drags, while Pakistan State Oil rode the crude spike to a rare gain. Volume thinned to 152.07 million shares (Rs17.72bn), with decliners beating advancers 81 to 18. The session came even as Islamabad and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on the fourth EFF and third RSF reviews on 7 October, unlocking roughly $1.2 billion pending Executive Board approval, while the rupee held broadly steady at 277.01 interbank, September CPI eased to 10.3% y/y and the SBP's 11.5% policy rate stayed on hold. Business Recorder and ProPakistani.
matrix.gcc_html: Gulf fundamentals strengthened on two fronts Thursday. Oil jumped as Iran escalated attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — Brent settled up 4.0% at $104.28 and WTI up 3.6% at $91.49 — a tailwind for Gulf budgets even as shippers and insurers price a heavier risk premium. Non-oil momentum held firm regardless: the UAE's S&P Global PMI stayed at 55.3 in September on the fastest output growth since February, and Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI rose to a seven-month high of 55.3 from 53.8 in August. Saudi's PIF approved its 2026–2030 strategy, tilting 80% of capital toward domestic sectors — tourism, NEOM, advanced manufacturing — as Vision 2030's diversification drive outpaces the oil-price swings. CNBC and ICIS.
matrix.global_html: Wall Street wobbled Thursday as the Hormuz-driven oil spike revived inflation fears and a Financial Times report trimming OpenAI's revenue estimate hit chipmakers: the S&P 500 fell 0.47% to 7,765.36 and the Nasdaq tumbled 1.25% to 27,193.34, while the Dow eked out a 0.10% gain to 51,231.64 on energy-stock strength. Treasury yields held near multi-decade highs (10-year ~5.23%, 2-year ~4.77%) after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said further hikes are "probably necessary," with futures pricing roughly 81–83% odds of an October hold but better-than-75% odds of a December hike, consistent with 16 of 18 FOMC members' dot-plot projections. Washington's funding risk is parked for now — the continuing resolution signed 2 September keeps the government funded through 11 December. Yahoo Finance and CNBC.

legislative.policy_html: IMF–Pakistan staff-level agreement on the fourth EFF review and third RSF review, reached 7 October, releasing roughly $1.2bn pending Executive Board approval.
legislative.sectors: Banks, FX Reserves, External Sector, Sovereign Bonds
legislative.impact_html: Wins: banks and FX reserves once the Executive Board clears the tranche, and sovereign bondholders on reduced near-term default risk. Loses: importers and consumers if the IMF's push for continued exchange-rate flexibility weighs on the rupee, and rate-sensitive borrowers given the SBP's 11.5% hold.

legislative.policy_html: UAE's 1 October VAT-refund and tax-evasion compliance rules alongside Saudi Arabia's PIF 2026–2030 strategy reallocating capital toward domestic sectors.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: large compliant corporates and banks absorbing new data-driven audits, and PIF-backed domestic tourism, NEOM and manufacturing assets. Loses: SMEs facing heavier VAT-chain verification costs, and foreign asset managers as PIF trims its foreign-allocation ceiling to 20% from a 30% peak.

legislative.policy_html: US continuing resolution funding the government through 11 December, alongside the Fed's hawkish dot-plot signalling a likely December hike.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: government contractors and bond-market stability from near-term funding certainty. Loses: growth and tech equities facing a higher-for-longer rate path, with a fresh shutdown fight looming once the stopgap expires in December.

levels.resistance_note: Wednesday's close; then Thursday's intraday high of 169,490

desk_stance_html: Thursday's reversal — a 2,045-point swing from intraday high to close — argues for a defensive bias into Friday: banks and fertilisers absorbed the bulk of the profit-taking, and with volume thinning to Rs17.72bn, we'd want to see participation rebuild before trusting a bounce back above 168,580. The IMF staff-level agreement is a genuine medium-term positive once the Executive Board ratifies it, but near-term price action is being set by the Hormuz-driven oil spike and a Fed that still leans toward a December hike. Our stance: hold core positions, avoid chasing strength into resistance, and watch Brent/WTI and Hormuz headlines as the swing factor for both the rupee and risk appetite. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.

linkedin_text:
KSE-100 sheds 1,138 points as Hormuz tanker attacks spike oil and rattle Wall Street — even as Pakistan locks in a $1.2bn IMF deal.

THE OVERNIGHT TAPE
US stocks closed mixed Thursday as Iran's escalating attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz sent Brent up 4.0% to $104.28 and WTI up 3.6% to $91.49, reviving inflation fears. The Nasdaq fell 1.25% to 27,193.34 and the S&P 500 lost 0.47% to 7,765.36, while the Dow edged up 0.10% to 51,231.64 on energy strength. Treasury yields held near multi-decade highs (10Y ~5.23%, 2Y ~4.77%) after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said further hikes are "probably necessary" — futures price ~81-83% odds of an October hold but better-than-75% odds of a December hike.

PAKISTAN
The KSE-100 fell 1,138.50 points (-0.68%) to 167,441.90, reversing from an intraday high of 169,486.60 as United Bank, Fauji Fertilizer, Systems Limited and Engro Fertilizers led the selling; Pakistan State Oil was a rare gainer on the crude spike. Volume thinned to 152.07m shares (Rs17.72bn). The pullback came despite genuine good news: Islamabad and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on 7 October on the fourth EFF and third RSF reviews, unlocking roughly $1.2bn pending Executive Board approval. The rupee held steady at 277.01 interbank, September CPI eased to 10.3% y/y, and the SBP's policy rate stayed on hold at 11.5%.

GCC
Gulf budgets caught a tailwind from the oil spike, while diversification kept humming: the UAE's S&P Global PMI held at 55.3 in September and Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI jumped to a seven-month high of 55.3 from 53.8. Saudi's PIF approved its 2026-2030 strategy, directing 80% of capital into domestic sectors — tourism, NEOM, advanced manufacturing — as foreign allocation is trimmed to 20% from a 30% peak.

GLOBAL
Washington's funding risk is on ice for now — the continuing resolution signed 2 September funds the government through 11 December — but the Fed's hawkish dot plot (16 of 18 members projecting a further 2026 hike) keeps rate-sensitive equities exposed, and a fresh shutdown fight looms once the stopgap lapses.

LEGISLATIVE TRACKER
• Pakistan: IMF staff-level deal unlocks ~$1.2bn — banks and FX reserves win; importers and borrowers face exchange-rate and rate risk.
• GCC: UAE VAT-compliance crackdown + Saudi PIF's domestic tilt — large compliant corporates and PIF-backed tourism/NEOM win; SMEs and foreign asset managers lose ground.
• Global: US funding certainty through 11 December vs. a likely December Fed hike — contractors and bonds stabilise; growth and tech equities stay exposed.

THE DAY AHEAD
KSE-100 support 166,500 (deeper support 165,000), pivot 167,442 (Thursday's close), resistance 168,580 then 169,490. Our stance: hold core positions, avoid chasing strength into resistance, and watch Brent/WTI and Hormuz headlines as the swing factor for both the rupee and risk appetite. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.
